claim: The COVID-19 pandemic has resulted in nearly 500 million infections and over 6,000,000 deaths.
source: The pandemic has impacted all parts of the globe and resulted in nearly 500 million infections and over 6,000,000 deaths (Dong et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Dong et al., 2020

claim: Approximately 14% of infected unvaccinated individuals develop severe COVID-19 disease requiring hospitalization.
source: Approximately 14% of infected unvaccinated individuals develop a severe clinical disease that requires hospitalization (Wu and McGoogan, 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wu and McGoogan, 2020

claim: The primary organ affected by severe COVID-19 is the lung.
source: While the primary organ affected by severe COVID-19 is the lung, many other organs, including the heart, liver, and kidney, are also affected (Mokhtari et al., 2020; Xie et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies

claim: Many organs including the heart, liver, and kidney are affected by COVID-19.
source: While the primary organ affected by severe COVID-19 is the lung, many other organs, including the heart, liver, and kidney, are also affected (Mokhtari et al., 2020; Xie et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to Mokhtari et al., 2020; Xie et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2021

claim: Long-COVID is more common in patients with a severe initial infection.
source: Long-COVID often affects multiple organs and is more common in patients with a severe initial infection (Taquet et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Taquet et al., 2021

claim: Viral infection stimulates macrophages to overproduce pro-inflammatory cytokines, including IL-6.
source: Viral infection stimulates macrophages to overproduce pro-inflammatory cytokines, including IL-6, leading to the 'cytokine storm' that results in systemic inflammatory response syndrome (Hu et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hu et al., 2021

claim: Macrophage overproduction of pro-inflammatory cytokines leads to a 'cytokine storm' that results in systemic inflammatory response syndrome.
source: Viral infection stimulates macrophages to overproduce pro-inflammatory cytokines, including IL-6, leading to the 'cytokine storm' that results in systemic inflammatory response syndrome (Hu et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hu et al., 2021

claim: Endothelial cells can be directly injured in response to pro-inflammatory cytokines.
source: This heightened inflammatory state affects multiple organs, partly through effects on endothelial cells, which can be directly injured in response to pro-inflammatory cytokines and produce a procoagulant state leading to thrombosis (Fard et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Fard et al., 2021

claim: Endothelial cells produce a procoagulant state leading to thrombosis in COVID-19.
source: This heightened inflammatory state affects multiple organs, partly through effects on endothelial cells, which can be directly injured in response to pro-inflammatory cytokines and produce a procoagulant state leading to thrombosis (Fard et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Fard et al., 2021

claim: The COVID Tissue Atlas comprises approximately 86,000 cells from six organs.
source: Here, we report a COVID-19 single-nuclei RNA-sequencing (snRNA-seq) atlas comprising six organs and approximately 86,000 cells.
evidence: Directly stated in the manuscript text

claim: Transcriptional changes in severe COVID-19 infections were not restricted to the lung but extended to multiple organs such as the liver and heart.
source: We showed that transcriptional changes in severe COVID-19 infections were not restricted to the lung, the most severely affected organ upon SARS-CoV-2 infection, but to multiple organs, such as the liver and heart.
evidence: Supported by data analysis presented in the manuscript

claim: The study collected organs from 20 different autopsies, of which 15 tested positive for COVID-19.
source: We collected data from 20 different autopsies (17 males, 3 females) with an age range between 40 and 89 years (median age = 68 years), of which 15 tested positive for COVID-19 (Figure 1A).
evidence: Directly stated in the manuscript text

claim: After quality control, 85,376 cells were deemed high quality and used to form the COVID Tissue Atlas.
source: After quality control, 85,376 cells (60,946 cells from COVID-19 samples and 24,430 cells from healthy donors) were deemed high quality and used to form the CTA (Figure 1B and C).
evidence: Directly stated in the manuscript text

claim: snRNA-seq is prone to high levels of ambient RNA contamination.
source: snRNA-seq is prone to high levels of ambient RNA contamination, which we corrected by applying an established correction algorithm (Fleming et al., 2019) along with filtering of doublets (Methods).
evidence: Supported by citation to Fleming et al., 2019 and established knowledge

claim: Measurements of SARS-CoV-2 mRNA by RT-qPCR showed high to moderate expression in the lung samples from COVID-19 donors.
source: Measurements of SARS-CoV-2 mRNA by RT-qPCR showed high to moderate expression in the lung samples from COVID-19 donors (Figure 1—figure supplement 4A).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4A

claim: Significant viral mRNA load was not detected by RT-qPCR in organs other than the lung.
source: While some of the COVID-19 associated genes such as ACE2, TMPRSS2, and NRP1 were expressed in multiple organs (Figure 1—figure supplement 4C), we did not detect significant viral mRNA load by RT-qPCR in the other organs processed (Figure 1—figure supplement 4A).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4A

claim: The CTA lung dataset comprised 21,474 cells, of which 11,790 were collected from COVID-19 autopsies.
source: The CTA lung dataset comprised 21,474 cells, of which 11,790 were collected from COVID-19 autopsies.
evidence: Directly stated in the manuscript text

claim: Ten distinct cell types were identified in the lung after quality control and clustering.
source: After quality control and clustering (Methods), we identified 10 distinct cell types, including primary epithelial and immune cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: Supported by data analysis and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, B

claim: Loss of AT1 and AT2 cells was identified in COVID-19 lungs relative to healthy controls.
source: Consistent with previous studies (Delorey et al., 2021; Melms et al., 2021), we identified loss of AT1 and AT2 cells in COVID-19 lungs relative to healthy controls (Figure 2D, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A), along with a significant expansion of basal cells (Figure 2D, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, and citations to Delorey et al., 2021; Melms et al., 2021

claim: A significant expansion of basal cells was observed in COVID-19 lungs.
source: Consistent with previous studies (Delorey et al., 2021; Melms et al., 2021), we identified loss of AT1 and AT2 cells in COVID-19 lungs relative to healthy controls (Figure 2D, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A), along with a significant expansion of basal cells (Figure 2D, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, and citations to Delorey et al., 2021; Melms et al., 2021

claim: AT2 cells serve as progenitors to generate new epithelial cells during alveolar injury.
source: During alveolar injury, AT2 cells are known to serve as progenitors to generate new epithelial cells.
evidence: Based on established scientific knowledge

claim: Alveolar basal intermediates (ABIs) are KRT17+/KRT5- basaloid cells identified in human idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis lungs.
source: These cells were first identified in single-cell studies as KRT17+/KRT5- basaloid cells in human idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF) lungs (Habermann et al., 2020) and independently shown by in vitro studies to arise from AT2 cells (Kathiriya et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citations to Habermann et al., 2020 and Kathiriya et al., 2022

claim: ABIs arise from AT2 cells.
source: These cells were first identified in single-cell studies as KRT17+/KRT5- basaloid cells in human idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF) lungs (Habermann et al., 2020) and independently shown by in vitro studies to arise from AT2 cells (Kathiriya et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kathiriya et al., 2022

claim: ABIs are present in the COVID-19 lung.
source: Thus, our data suggest that ABIs (Kathiriya et al., 2022) are present in the COVID-19 lung, and their trans-differentiation from endogenous AT2s could account for the gain of abnormal basal cells in the alveoli, which are lost in COVID-19 lungs.
evidence: Inferred from data analysis comparing CTA with reference datasets

claim: Trans-differentiation of ABIs from endogenous AT2s could account for the gain of abnormal basal cells in the alveoli in COVID-19 lungs.
source: Thus, our data suggest that ABIs (Kathiriya et al., 2022) are present in the COVID-19 lung, and their trans-differentiation from endogenous AT2s could account for the gain of abnormal basal cells in the alveoli, which are lost in COVID-19 lungs.
evidence: Speculative interpretation based on data analysis

claim: Hepatocytes comprised around 60% of cells in healthy liver samples and more than 80% in COVID-19 liver samples.
source: Across all six cell types identified in the liver (Figure 3A), hepatocytes comprised around 60% of cells in the healthy samples and more than 80% in the COVID-19 samples (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3B

claim: Approximately 20% of cells from healthy liver samples were annotated as endothelial as opposed to less than 10% in COVID-19 donors.
source: However, we observed an inverse trend for endothelial cells, where approximately 20% of the cells from healthy samples were annotated as endothelial as opposed to less than 10% in COVID-19 donors, which may reflect recently reported endotheliopathy in COVID-19 livers (McConnell et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by data analysis and citation to McConnell et al., 2021

claim: Hepatocytes, endothelial cells, and macrophages showed the largest number of differentially expressed genes in COVID-19 liver donors.
source: Across all cell types, hepatocytes, endothelial cells, and macrophages showed the largest number of DE genes in COVID-19 donors (more than 200 up-regulated genes with an average log2-FC >2 and adjusted-p <1e-6; Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by differential expression analysis shown in Figure 3C

claim: Dysregulation in the insulin signaling pathway was found in hepatocytes, macrophages, and endothelial cells from COVID-19 livers.
source: We found dysregulation in the insulin signaling pathway in hepatocytes, macrophages, and endothelial cells from COVID-19 livers (Supplementary file 3; p<1e-6).
evidence: Supported by pathway enrichment analysis

claim: Patients with type 2 diabetes have worse outcomes with severe COVID-19 infection.
source: Patients with type 2 diabetes have worse outcomes with severe COVID-19 infection (Xie and Al-Aly, 2022), and clinical studies show aberrant glucose levels in SARS-CoV2 infected patients with type 2 diabetes (Reiterer et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to Xie and Al-Aly, 2022 and Reiterer et al., 2021

claim: Clinical studies show aberrant glucose levels in SARS-CoV2 infected patients with type 2 diabetes.
source: Patients with type 2 diabetes have worse outcomes with severe COVID-19 infection (Xie and Al-Aly, 2022), and clinical studies show aberrant glucose levels in SARS-CoV2 infected patients with type 2 diabetes (Reiterer et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Reiterer et al., 2021

claim: Dysregulated insulin signaling in hepatocytes might explain why SARS-CoV2 infected patients with type 2 diabetes have uncontrolled glucose homeostasis.
source: Thus, our data suggest that dysregulated insulin signaling – especially in hepatocytes, which play a critical role in maintaining glucose homeostasis (Klover and Mooney, 2004) – might explain why SARS-CoV2 infected patients with type 2 diabetes have uncontrolled glucose homeostasis and are comorbid (Mishra and Dey, 2021) and why COVID-19 infection could lead to the development of type 2 diabetes (Barrett et al., 2022).
evidence: Speculative interpretation based on data analysis and citations

claim: COVID-19 infection could lead to the development of type 2 diabetes.
source: Thus, our data suggest that dysregulated insulin signaling – especially in hepatocytes, which play a critical role in maintaining glucose homeostasis (Klover and Mooney, 2004) – might explain why SARS-CoV2 infected patients with type 2 diabetes have uncontrolled glucose homeostasis and are comorbid (Mishra and Dey, 2021) and why COVID-19 infection could lead to the development of type 2 diabetes (Barrett et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to Barrett et al., 2022 and speculative interpretation

claim: Heart samples yielded 20,091 cells after quality control from 11 donors.
source: Heart samples yielded 20,091 cells after quality control (n=11 donors) (Figure 4A).
evidence: Directly stated in the manuscript text

claim: The large majority of heart cells corresponded to endothelial cells, cardiomyocytes, and fibroblasts.
source: Across the eight cell types identified, the large majority of cells corresponded to endothelial cells (>40% in COVID-19 samples, 13% in healthy samples), cardiomyocytes (25% in COVID-19 samples, 28% in healthy samples), and fibroblasts (15% in COVID-19 samples, 45% in healthy samples) (Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4B

claim: An increase in the relative composition of capillary and aerocyte endothelial sub-classes was observed in COVID-19 lung samples.
source: We then compared the relative composition of endothelial sub-cell types in healthy and COVID-19 samples and noticed an increase in the relative composition of capillary and aerocyte sub-classes (Figure 3—figure supplement 2f).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2f

claim: Angiogenesis genes are significantly up-regulated in capillary endothelial cells in COVID-19 lungs.
source: Consistent with this, gene ontology (GO) analysis of the DE genes from capillary endothelial cells in the lungs showed that angiogenesis genes are significantly up-regulated (Figure 3—figure supplement 2h).
evidence: Supported by GO analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2h

claim: Cardiomyocytes, endothelial cells, and macrophages showed significant transcriptional changes in COVID-19 heart samples.
source: We then found significant transcriptional changes in cardiomyocytes, endothelial cells, and macrophages based on the number of DE genes in COVID-19 samples (Figure 4C).
evidence: Supported by differential expression analysis shown in Figure 4C

claim: Insulin pathway enrichment was observed in cardiomyocytes from COVID-19 samples.
source: Similar to the liver, we observed insulin pathway enrichment in cardiomyocytes from COVID-19 samples (Figure 4C).
evidence: Supported by pathway enrichment analysis shown in Figure 4C

claim: Heart failure is associated with generalized insulin resistance.
source: Heart failure is associated with generalized insulin resistance.
evidence: Based on established scientific knowledge

claim: Insulin-resistant states such as type 2 diabetes mellitus and obesity increase the risk of heart failure.
source: Moreover, insulin-resistant states such as type 2 diabetes mellitus and obesity increase the risk of heart failure even after adjusting for traditional risk factors (Riehle and Abel, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Riehle and Abel, 2016

claim: COVID-19 triggers insulin resistance in patients, causing chronic metabolic disorders that were non-existent before infection.
source: In agreement with our data, other studies found that COVID-19 triggers insulin resistance in patients, causing chronic metabolic disorders that were non-existent before infection (Govender et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Govender et al., 2021

claim: Significant changes in Notch, Hippo, and MAPK signaling pathways were observed in cardiomyocytes from COVID-19 samples.
source: Additionally, we observed significant changes in Notch, Hippo, and MAPK signaling pathways in cardiomyocytes from COVID-19 samples (Figure 4D).
evidence: Supported by pathway enrichment analysis shown in Figure 4D

claim: BMP and TGFβ signaling pathways showed specific down-regulation in endothelial cells from COVID-19 hearts.
source: Conversely, the BMP and TGFβ signaling pathways showed specific down-regulation in endothelial cells from COVID-19 hearts, including down-regulation of BMPR1A, BMPR1B, SMAD6, and BMP6 (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: Supported by pathway enrichment analysis

claim: Notch signaling has been proposed as a target to prevent SARS-CoV-2 infection and interfere with the progression of COVID-19 associated heart and lung disease.
source: Interestingly, Notch signaling has been proposed as a target to prevent SARS-CoV-2 infection and interfere with the progression of COVID-19 associated heart and lung disease (Rizzo et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Rizzo et al., 2020

claim: Hippo signaling is involved in the development of many diseases caused by viruses.
source: Recent studies indicate that Hippo signaling is involved in the development of many diseases caused by viruses.
evidence: Based on recent studies

claim: TGFβ signaling is linked to the response of endothelial cells to inflammation in COVID-19.
source: Finally, TGFβ signaling is linked to the response of endothelial cells to inflammation in COVID-19 (Yoshimatsu and Watabe, 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to Yoshimatsu and Watabe, 2022

claim: A significant overlap in differentially expressed genes was found in macrophages across organs compared to random sampling expectations.
source: In macrophages, we found a significant overlap in DE genes across organs compared to random sampling expectations (Figure 5A).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 5A

claim: A set of 89 differentially expressed genes was found in COVID-19 macrophages from all three organs (lung, liver, heart).
source: Specifically, we found a set of 89 DE genes in COVID-19 macrophages from all three organs, including PLCG2, HIF1A, ACTB, and JUND.
evidence: Supported by cross-organ differential expression analysis

claim: The shared transcriptional response of endothelial cells from COVID-19 samples showed the highest coordination across multiple pairs of organs.
source: The STR of endothelial cells from COVID-19 samples showed the highest coordination across multiple pairs of organs (Figure 5G).
evidence: Supported by coordination score analysis shown in Figure 5G

claim: Significant coordination was found in macrophages across the liver, lung, and heart.
source: We also found significant coordination in macrophages across the liver, lung, and heart (z-score >5; Figure 5G).
evidence: Supported by coordination score analysis shown in Figure 5G

claim: The shared transcriptional response of fibroblasts and stromal cells showed no significant coordination compared to the randomized control.
source: In contrast, the STR of fibroblasts and stromal cells showed no significant coordination compared to the randomized control, possibly due to the low number of overlapping DE genes (Figure 5G and Figures 3C and 4C).
evidence: Supported by coordination score analysis shown in Figure 5G

claim: From 125 significantly expressed genes found in the shared transcriptional response of macrophages in the CTA, 65 also appeared in the Broad atlas, representing a 52% overlap across datasets.
source: From 125 significantly expressed genes found in the SRT response of macrophages in the CTA, 65 also appeared in the Broad atlas, representing a 52% overlap across datasets (equivalently, we found a 31% overlap for the SRT in endothelial cells – Supplementary file 7).
evidence: Supported by cross-dataset validation analysis

claim: COVID-19 infection induces coordinated transcriptional regulation in macrophages and endothelial cells across multiple organs.
source: Together, these results indicate that COVID-19 infection induces coordinated transcriptional regulation in macrophages and endothelial cells across multiple organs.
evidence: Inferred from coordination analysis across organs

claim: The HIF-1 pathway showed high fold enrichment in macrophages across all organs.
source: The HIF-1 pathway showed high fold enrichment across all organs (Figure 6A), suggesting a pivotal role of macrophages in the systemic response to oxygen homeostasis in COVID-19.
evidence: Supported by pathway enrichment analysis shown in Figure 6A

claim: The Notch pathway was enriched in macrophages from all three organs.
source: The Notch pathway was also enriched in macrophages from all three organs (Figure 6A), confirming that Notch signaling has a crucial role in the systemic response to COVID-19 (Breikaa and Lilly, 2021; Farahani et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by pathway enrichment analysis shown in Figure 6A and citations

claim: Multiple enriched pathways were found in the coordinated shared transcriptional response of endothelial cells, including Notch and Ephrin signaling in the lung, liver, and heart.
source: In the coordinated STR of endothelial cells, we found multiple enriched pathways, including Notch and Ephrin signaling in the lung, liver, and heart (Figure 6B).
evidence: Supported by pathway enrichment analysis shown in Figure 6B

claim: VEGF signaling was enriched in liver and heart endothelial cells from COVID-19 samples.
source: Additionally, we found enrichment for VEGF signaling in liver and heart (p<1e-3, and lung p<1e-2; Supplementary file 6).
evidence: Supported by pathway enrichment analysis

claim: VEGF-D was identified as the most predictive indicator for the severity of COVID-19.
source: A recent study using measurements of growth factors and cytokines in serum identified VEGF-D as the most predictive indicator for the severity of COVID-19 (Kong et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kong et al., 2020

claim: VEGF was proposed as a promising therapeutic target for suppressing inflammation during SARS-CoV-2 infection.
source: Similarly, VEGF was proposed as a promising therapeutic target for suppressing inflammation during SARS-CoV-2 infection (Yin et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Yin et al., 2020

claim: Changes in VEGF signaling in COVID-19 donors are not necessarily organ-specific but rather part of a systemic response of endothelial cells.
source: Our results indicate that changes in VEGF signaling in COVID-19 donors are not necessarily organ-specific but rather part of a systemic response of endothelial cells and, therefore, of relevance for the development of treatments and as potential drug targets.
evidence: Inferred from cross-organ pathway enrichment analysis

claim: Multiple enriched ligand-receptor pairs were identified between macrophages and endothelial cells in all three organs from COVID-19 autopsies.
source: Multiple enriched ligand-receptor pairs were identified between macrophages and endothelial cells in all three organs from COVID-19 autopsies (23 ligand-receptor pairs in the heart, 13 in the liver, and 7 in the lung, p<1e-2; Figure 6C–E).
evidence: Supported by CellPhoneDB analysis shown in Figure 6C–E

claim: Expression of VEGF ligand-receptor pairs was found in the liver and heart.
source: Among the top signaling interactions, we found expression of VEGF ligand-receptor pairs in the liver and heart (FLT4:VEGFC; VEGFA: KDR; NRP2:VEGFA; VEGFA:FLT1).
evidence: Supported by ligand-receptor analysis

claim: Multiple Notch ligand-receptor enriched pairs involving the expression of the Dll4 ligand in endothelial cells were found in the heart.
source: In the heart, we found multiple Notch ligand-receptor enriched pairs involving the expression of the Dll4 ligand in endothelial cells (Figure 6D).
evidence: Supported by ligand-receptor analysis shown in Figure 6D

claim: The expression of Notch receptors in the heart was cell-type dependent: endothelial cells expressed Notch4 and Notch1, whereas macrophages expressed Notch2.
source: Interestingly, the expression of Notch receptors was cell-type dependent: endothelial cells expressed Notch4 and Notch1, whereas macrophages expressed Notch2 (Figure 6D).
evidence: Supported by ligand-receptor analysis shown in Figure 6D

claim: A Dll4-dependent signaling mechanism involving endothelial cells and macrophages in the COVID-19 heart is potentially related to HIF-1 signaling.
source: A Dll4-dependent signaling mechanism involving endothelial cells and macrophages in the COVID-19 heart is potentially related to HIF-1 signaling since these pathways are known to cross-talk through multiple mechanisms (Breikaa and Lilly, 2021; Zheng et al., 2008).
evidence: Speculative interpretation based on data and citations

claim: COVID-19 infection damages multiple organs.
source: Our study found that COVID-19 infection damages multiple organs, and our analyses reveal transcriptomic changes in various cell types across these organs.
evidence: Supported by comprehensive data analysis across organs

claim: The lungs are the most affected organ in COVID-19 infection.
source: While the lungs are the most affected organ in COVID-19 infection, our data shows widespread transcriptional changes related to cell signaling across multiple organs and cell types (Figure 5).
evidence: Based on data analysis and established knowledge

claim: Dysregulated insulin and HIF signaling were identified in the liver and heart.
source: Notably, we localized these signaling changes in two affected organs: the liver and heart, where we identified dysregulated insulin and HIF signaling and prominent potential macrophage-endothelial interactions (Figure 6).
evidence: Supported by pathway enrichment analysis shown in Figure 6

claim: Prominent potential macrophage-endothelial interactions were identified in the liver and heart.
source: Notably, we localized these signaling changes in two affected organs: the liver and heart, where we identified dysregulated insulin and HIF signaling and prominent potential macrophage-endothelial interactions (Figure 6).
evidence: Supported by ligand-receptor analysis shown in Figure 6

claim: A coordinated signature was identified in macrophages and endothelial cells by analyzing transcriptional changes in multiple organs.
source: Here, we present a cross-organ analysis of DE in the context of COVID-19. We identified a coordinated signature in macrophages and endothelial cells by analyzing the transcriptional changes in multiple organs, which is often overlooked in other studies.
evidence: Supported by cross-organ coordination analysis

claim: Coordinated signatures between macrophages and endothelial cells may be mediated by the known effects of the dysregulated immune system in the context and sequelae of COVID-19 infection.
source: These coordinated signatures between macrophages and endothelial cells may be mediated by the known effects of the dysregulated immune system in the context and sequelae of COVID-19 infection.
evidence: Speculative interpretation based on data and established knowledge

claim: One limitation of the study is the limited number of high-quality sequenced cells.
source: One limitation of our study is the limited number of high-quality sequenced cells. Despite initially targeting 1 million nuclei, most samples did not pass quality control.
evidence: Directly stated as a limitation

claim: The atlas is composed of single-nuclei samples, impeding the observation of some transcriptional effects in the cytoplasm due to technological limitations.
source: Another consideration is that our atlas is composed of single-nuclei samples, impeding the observation of some transcriptional effects in the cytoplasm due to technological limitations.
evidence: Directly stated as a limitation based on technical knowledge

claim: Insulin signaling dysregulation may contribute to developing diabetes in COVID-19 patients.
source: For example, insulin signaling dysregulation may contribute to developing diabetes in COVID-19 patients (Mishra and Dey, 2021).
evidence: Speculative interpretation based on data and citation

claim: Long-COVID appears to be a complex set of symptoms with variable organ dysfunction.
source: Long-COVID, which appears to be a complex set of symptoms with variable organ dysfunction (Morrow et al., 2022), may also be informed by our understanding of cellular changes across multiple tissues.
evidence: Supported by citation to Morrow et al., 2022
